1.title: Moses Is Dead, and Joshua Is Called
1.context: Joshua had served as Moses' assistant for forty years. The charge he receives repeats one sentence three times, and ties courage to keeping the Book of the Law Moses left behind.
1.question: When a responsibility passes to you, what helps you be strong and courageous rather than afraid?

1.title: Three Days, and an Oath Honored
1.context: The tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh already held land east of the Jordan, given by Moses on the condition that their fighting men cross over and help their brothers first (Numbers 32).
1.question: What promises have you made that cost you something to keep?

1.title: Two Spies and a House in the Wall
1.context: Jericho was a walled city near the Jordan crossing. Rahab's house stood in the city wall, and the flax on her roof was a normal part of flax processing, drying in the sun.
1.question: Rahab had only heard reports about Israel's God. What reports about God have reached you from far away?

1.title: The Confession on the Roof
1.context: Rahab's words about God in the heavens above and on the earth below echo what Moses taught Israel in Deuteronomy 4:39. The scarlet cord in her window becomes the sign her family will be spared by.
1.question: Rahab acted on what she had heard before she saw anything herself. Where might you need to do the same?

1.title: Follow the Ark
1.context: The ark of the covenant was the gold-covered chest holding the tablets of the law, carried by priests. Two thousand cubits is roughly half a mile, a gap so the whole nation could see the ark lead the way.
1.question: What does it look like to let God go first into a place you have never traveled before?

1.title: The River Stops at Flood Stage
1.context: The Jordan overflows its banks at harvest time, so the crossing happened at the river's highest water, not its lowest. The town of Adam, where the water backed up, lay many miles upstream.
1.question: Where have you seen God act at the hardest point of a situation rather than the easiest?

1.title: Twelve Stones from the Riverbed
1.context: Memorial stones are a pattern in this book. One set of twelve was carried to the camp at Gilgal; Joshua set up a second set in the middle of the river itself, where the priests had stood.
1.question: What has God done that you would want the next generation to ask about?

1.title: Gilgal, and the Question Children Will Ask
1.context: The crossing date, the tenth day of the first month, is the same date Israel had chosen Passover lambs in Egypt a generation earlier (Exodus 12:3). Gilgal became Israel's base camp east of Jericho.
1.question: How do you want to answer when someone asks what God has done for you?

2.title: Gilgal, and the Commander
2.context: Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham (Genesis 17). The wilderness generation had let it lapse for their sons. The manna ending the day after Passover marks the exact handoff from wilderness food to the land's own produce.
2.question: What old provision might God be ending because a new one has begun?

2.title: The Silent March
2.context: Rams' horns, called shofars, were used to signal in worship and war. The march repeated for six days, and the silence Joshua commanded broke only at the shout on the seventh day.
2.question: What is the hardest part of obeying an instruction that looks nothing like a solution?

2.title: The Wall Falls, and Rahab Is Kept
2.context: Things devoted to destruction were set apart wholly for God and could not be taken as personal plunder. Joshua's curse on rebuilding Jericho is recorded as fulfilled centuries later in 1 Kings 16:34.
2.question: Rahab's whole family was saved because of one person's faith and one window's cord. Who might be carried by your faithfulness?

2.title: The Secret in the Camp
2.context: Ai was a much smaller town than Jericho, near Bethel. The reader learns Achan's secret in the chapter's first verse, while Israel's army learns it only through defeat.
2.question: What hidden thing can quietly undo a whole group's strength?

2.title: Facedown, and God's Answer
2.context: Tearing clothes and putting dust on the head were signs of mourning and grief. Joshua's prayer ends by appealing to God's great name, the same appeal Moses made after the golden calf (Exodus 32).
2.question: When something goes wrong, do you pray more like Joshua here, blaming, confessing, or asking what happened?

2.title: The Lot Narrows to One Man
2.context: Casting lots was Israel's way of seeking God's decision in a matter. The valley's name, Achor, means trouble, and Achan's confession names what he saw, coveted, and took, in that order.
2.question: Achan's fall went from seeing, to wanting, to taking. Where is the wisest place to stop that chain in your own life?

2.title: Ai Taken by Ambush
2.context: This time God permits Israel to take Ai's plunder and livestock, which shows the Jericho ban was about that city's devoted status, not a permanent rule against plunder. The battle lance Joshua held out was a signal visible to the ambush force.
2.question: What failure in your life looks different when you approach it a second time with help?

2.title: The Law Read Between the Mountains
2.context: Moses had commanded this ceremony years earlier (Deuteronomy 27), with half the tribes on Mount Gerizim and half on Mount Ebal, facing each other across the valley where Shechem would stand.
2.question: Why do you think Israel stopped a war to hold a reading? What would that pause look like in your life?

3.title: The Embassy of Moldy Bread
3.context: Gibeon was a Hivite city only a day's walk from Gilgal. Its envoys recited what God had done in Egypt and east of the Jordan, striking details that were already a generation old.
3.question: Have you ever been persuaded by appearances that were carefully arranged?

3.title: The Oath Holds
3.context: An oath sworn by the LORD's name bound the swearer even when it had been won by deception. Israel later suffered a famine for breaking this very treaty (2 Samuel 21), which shows how seriously the oath was held.
3.question: What commitment have you made that you must honor even though it was entered badly?

3.title: Five Kings Against Gibeon
3.context: Beth-horon sits on a ridge road west of Gibeon; the descent toward Azekah drops into the foothills. Joshua's army marched uphill all night from Gilgal, roughly twenty miles, and arrived by surprise at dawn.
3.question: What does loyalty require of you when keeping your word becomes expensive?

3.title: The Long Day and the Cave
3.context: The Book of Jashar was an early collection of Israelite songs and records, quoted here by the narrator and also in 2 Samuel 1. The text presents the lengthened day through that source's words.
3.question: Joshua asked God for more time in front of everyone. What bold, specific thing might you ask God for openly?

3.title: The Southern Campaign
3.context: Commanders placing their feet on the necks of defeated kings was an ancient victory gesture. The campaign's city list covers the southern hill country and foothills in a single sweep before the return to Gilgal.
3.question: The kings were dealt with at sunset each time, as the law required for hanged men (Deuteronomy 21:23). Why might small obediences matter in the middle of big victories?

4.title: Chariots at the Waters of Merom
4.context: Hazor, north of the Sea of Galilee, was one of the largest cities in Canaan and head of a northern alliance. Horses and chariots were the advanced weapons of the age, and Israel had neither.
4.question: What do you do when the opposition in front of you is bigger and better equipped than you are?

4.title: Hazor Burned, and the Long War
4.context: Cities built on mounds, called tells, were layers of earlier cities. Hazor alone among them was burned. The summary also says the war took a long period of time, a different tempo from the southern campaign.
4.question: Which season are you in right now, a fast campaign or a long war, and what does faithfulness look like in it?

4.title: The Land Has Rest from War
4.context: The Anakim were the tall people whose size had terrified the first spies (Numbers 13). A remnant survived only in the Philistine cities of Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod, where a later generation would meet Goliath of Gath.
4.question: What fear from an earlier season of your life has lost its power over you?

4.title: Two Kings East of the Jordan
4.context: Sihon and Og were defeated under Moses, before the Jordan crossing (Numbers 21). Their land, from the Arnon to Mount Hermon, was the inheritance of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh.
4.question: Why is it worth remembering victories that happened before your time?

4.title: Thirty-One Kings
4.context: The list reads like one of the book's stone memorials, evidence in name form. Several cities in it, like Bethel and Tappuah, appear without a narrated battle, so the list preserves more than the story told.
4.question: What would your own list of God's victories include, name by name?

5.title: Very Much of the Land Remains
5.context: God's list of remaining land includes the five Philistine cities and the Sidonian coast, territory Israel would still be contesting in the days of the judges and kings. The eastern survey repeats that Levi receives no territory.
5.question: What unfinished work has God named plainly in your life, and what is your next step into it?

5.title: Caleb Speaks, and Receives Hebron
5.context: Caleb was from Judah, and his fellow spy Joshua was the only other man of their generation still living. His speech quotes the oath Moses swore at Kadesh-barnea forty-five years earlier (Numbers 14 and Deuteronomy 1).
5.question: Caleb asked for the hardest portion, not the easiest. What would asking boldly look like for you?

5.title: Caleb Collects, Achsah Asks, and Judah's Towns
5.context: Achsah's springs made dry Negev land livable; water was the difference between a deed and a home. The chapter's closing note about Jerusalem's Jebusites stays true until David takes the city generations later (2 Samuel 5).
5.question: Achsah asked her father for what the gift still lacked. What would you ask God for to complete a good gift?

6.title: Joseph's Portion, Five Sisters, and a Rebuke
6.context: Zelophehad's daughters had won their inheritance ruling from God through Moses in Numbers 27, and the ruling against marrying outside the tribe followed in Numbers 36. Gezer and Megiddo guarded major trade routes, which is part of why they held out.
6.question: Caleb asked for giants; Joseph's sons asked for land without a fight. Which request is closer to your own prayers lately?

6.title: The Survey and the Lots at Shiloh
6.context: Shiloh, in Ephraim's hills, became Israel's central sanctuary town, where the Tent of Meeting stood for generations. The surveyors' written map is one of the earliest land surveys described in the Bible.
6.question: Joshua's question, how long will you put off, is aimed at delay. Where is delay costing you ground?

6.title: Cities of Refuge, Cities for Levi
6.context: The refuge system protected the accidental killer from revenge until a fair hearing, a law first given in Numbers 35. The forty-eight Levitical cities spread the priestly tribe through every other tribe's territory.
6.question: What protections do the vulnerable have because someone obeyed an unglamorous command?

6.title: Not One Promise Failed
6.context: These verses are the allotment section's verdict. They speak of God's side of the story, the giving of the land, while the same chapters honestly record where Israel's possession still lagged behind the gift.
6.question: Which of God's promises can you say, from your own experience, has not failed?

7.title: Released with a Blessing
7.context: The eastern tribes' men had been away from their families for the whole conquest, years of fighting for their brothers' inheritance under the agreement made in Numbers 32 and renewed in Joshua 1.
7.question: What does it mean to finish a long obligation well and be sent home with a charge to hold fast?

7.title: An Imposing Altar
7.context: Altars in Israel's law belonged at the one place God chose (Deuteronomy 12), so a second great altar looked like the start of a rival worship. The congregation gathered at Shiloh, where the Tent of Meeting stood.
7.question: What have you judged quickly from a distance that deserved a closer look?

7.title: The Embassy Accuses
7.context: Phinehas had stopped the plague at Peor with decisive action (Numbers 25). The embassy's offer to share western land was real generosity inside an accusation: they would give up inheritance rather than see the nation split in worship.
7.question: How do you confront someone you believe is wrong, in a way that leaves them a way back?

7.title: Built Out of Fear, and Named Witness
7.context: The eastern tribes' fear was about identity across a natural border: that a river on a map would become a boundary of belonging for their grandchildren. A replica altar could preach without ever being used for sacrifice.
7.question: What could you build or record now that would speak faithfully to people you will never meet?

8.title: The First Farewell
8.context: Joshua 23 is spoken to Israel's leaders after a long rest; Joshua 24 gathers all the tribes at Shechem. The charge not to turn to the right or to the left repeats God's own words to Joshua in Joshua 1:7.
8.question: What charge would you pass on if you had one speech left to give?

8.title: Snares, and the Way of All the Earth
8.context: The warning focuses on slow assimilation, intermarriage and shared worship, rather than military threat. Joshua's phrase for his death, going the way of all the earth, is also used by David in 1 Kings 2:2.
8.question: Which of Joshua's two faces of the same promise, blessing or calamity, do you need to hear more clearly?

8.title: God Retells the Story
8.context: Shechem sits between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, where the law was read in Joshua 8. God's recital is told in the first person and covers ground the reader has traveled from Genesis to this chapter.
8.question: If God retold your story in the first person, which I took, I gave, I brought moments would stand out?

8.title: Choose This Day
8.context: The choice Joshua names is between the gods from beyond the Euphrates, the gods of Egypt, and the gods of the Amorites around them, the old worlds behind and the new world in front.
8.question: What would choosing this day look like in one concrete area of your life?

8.title: The Vow, Priced and Given
8.context: Joshua's resistance to a quick vow makes the people's pledge deliberate. The great stone under the oak becomes the final memorial of the book, a witness that has, in the text's words, heard all the words spoken there.
8.question: When has someone done you the kindness of slowing down a promise before you made it?

8.title: Three Burials
8.context: Joshua dies at 110, Joseph's age at death in Genesis 50, and is buried in the town he requested. Joseph's bones fulfill the oath sworn in Genesis 50:25 and carried out of Egypt in Exodus 13:19. Eleazar's burial completes the priestly generation.
8.question: Joseph's burial waited centuries for a promise to land. What long promise are you still carrying, and what keeps you carrying it?
